questions.question: What is Spring Boot, and how does it differ from the Spring Framework?
questions.answer: Spring Framework is the underlying dependency-injection and infrastructure framework (Core, MVC, Data, Security, etc.) that requires developers to explicitly wire beans, configure a DispatcherServlet, set up a DataSource, and deploy to an external server. Spring Boot is built on top of the Spring Framework and is an 'opinionated' layer that removes that manual setup: it provides auto-configuration (guessing sensible beans based on what's on the classpath), starter dependencies (curated dependency bundles like spring-boot-starter-web), an embedded servlet container (Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow) so the app runs as a standalone executable JAR, and production-ready features via Actuator. In short: Spring Framework is the toolkit; Spring Boot is the fast, convention-over-configuration way to bootstrap and run a Spring application with minimal boilerplate. A common interview follow-up is that Spring Boot doesn't replace Spring - every Spring Boot app is still a full Spring application underneath.

questions.question: What does the @SpringBootApplication annotation do?
questions.answer: @SpringBootApplication is a convenience meta-annotation that combines three separate annotations: @Configuration (marks the class as a source of bean definitions), @ComponentScan (scans the current package and sub-packages for @Component/@Service/@Repository/@Controller beans), and @EnableAutoConfiguration (triggers Spring Boot's auto-configuration mechanism, which registers beans based on what's on the classpath and what properties are set). Internally, @EnableAutoConfiguration works by loading auto-configuration classes declared in metadata (an AutoConfiguration.imports file in modern Spring Boot versions), each guarded by conditional annotations like @ConditionalOnClass and @ConditionalOnMissingBean, so a bean is only created when its prerequisites are present and the user hasn't already defined one. Placing @SpringBootApplication on the main class also fixes the 'base package' used for component scanning - a common gotcha is that classes outside that package tree won't be picked up unless you widen @ComponentScan explicitly.

questions.question: What are Spring Boot starters, and can you name a few you've used?
questions.answer: Starters are curated dependency descriptors - Maven/Gradle artifacts named spring-boot-starter-* - that pull in a consistent, tested set of libraries for a given purpose so you don't have to hunt down compatible versions yourself. For example, spring-boot-starter-web brings in Spring MVC, an embedded Tomcat, and Jackson for JSON; spring-boot-starter-data-jpa brings in Spring Data JPA and Hibernate; spring-boot-starter-security brings in Spring Security; spring-boot-starter-test brings in JUnit, Mockito, and AssertJ; spring-boot-starter-actuator adds production monitoring endpoints. Because they're managed through the Spring Boot BOM (Bill of Materials), you generally don't specify explicit versions for the transitive libraries - Boot's parent POM/BOM keeps them mutually compatible, which avoids the classic 'dependency hell' of mismatched library versions.

questions.question: What is the difference between @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Controller?
questions.answer: All four are stereotype annotations built on top of @Component, so Spring's component scan treats them identically for the purpose of registering a bean - functionally, they're interchangeable at the container level. The difference is semantic and, for @Repository, also functional: @Component is the generic marker for any Spring-managed bean; @Service signals a class holding business logic (purely a documentation/intent convention, no extra behavior); @Controller marks a class as a Spring MVC web controller whose methods typically return view names (use @RestController, which combines @Controller + @ResponseBody, for REST APIs that return data directly); @Repository marks a class as a data-access object and additionally enables Spring's PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor, which translates persistence-technology-specific exceptions (e.g., Hibernate's exceptions) into Spring's unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy, so callers can catch a consistent exception type regardless of the underlying ORM. Using the more specific stereotype where it applies (rather than always @Component) makes the codebase self-documenting and, in @Repository's case, gives you real added behavior.

questions.question: What is the difference between @RestController and @Controller?
questions.answer: @Controller is the base Spring MVC stereotype for a web controller; by default, the String or ModelAndView a handler method returns is resolved as a view name (e.g., a Thymeleaf template) via a ViewResolver. @RestController is a composed annotation equal to @Controller + @ResponseBody: it tells Spring to write the return value of every handler method directly to the HTTP response body (serialized as JSON/XML via an HttpMessageConverter like Jackson) instead of resolving it as a view name. In practice, @RestController is what you use for REST APIs, and @Controller is what you use for server-rendered web pages; you can still add @ResponseBody to individual methods in a @Controller class if you want a mix of view-returning and data-returning endpoints in the same class.

questions.question: What is the default embedded server in Spring Boot, and how do you change the port it listens on?
questions.answer: Spring Boot auto-configures an embedded web server purely based on what's on the classpath - if spring-boot-starter-web is present, it defaults to embedded Apache Tomcat. To use Jetty or Undertow instead, you exclude the Tomcat starter dependency and add spring-boot-starter-jetty or spring-boot-starter-undertow; Boot's auto-configuration detects the swap and configures the new server automatically, no code changes required. To change the port, set server.port in application.properties/application.yml (server.port=9090), pass it as a command-line argument (--server.port=9090), or set an environment variable (SERVER_PORT=9090). Setting server.port=0 tells Boot to pick a random free port, which is commonly used in integration tests to avoid port collisions.

questions.question: What is dependency injection, and what are the ways Spring supports injecting dependencies?
questions.answer: Dependency Injection (DI) is the pattern where an object's dependencies are supplied by an external container rather than the object creating or looking them up itself - it's the concrete implementation of Inversion of Control (IoC). Instead of `new`-ing up a UserRepository inside a UserService, the Spring container constructs the UserRepository bean and hands it to UserService, which decouples the two and makes the service trivially testable (you can inject a mock). Spring supports three injection styles: constructor injection (dependencies passed via the constructor - the recommended default, since it allows fields to be final and makes missing dependencies fail fast at startup), setter injection (dependencies set via setter methods - useful for optional dependencies), and field injection (dependencies injected directly into fields via @Autowired - the most concise but generally discouraged because it hides dependencies, prevents immutability, and makes unit testing without a Spring context harder).

questions.question: What is the default bean scope in Spring, and what other scopes are available?
questions.answer: The default bean scope is singleton - one shared instance per Spring container (application context), reused for every injection point. Other built-in scopes are: prototype (a new instance is created every time the bean is requested/injected); and, for web-aware application contexts, request (one instance per HTTP request), session (one instance per HTTP session), and application (one instance per ServletContext). A key gotcha is injecting a shorter-lived scoped bean (e.g., request-scoped) into a singleton bean directly - you need a scoped proxy (proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS on @Scope) so the singleton holds a proxy that resolves to the correct instance for the current request/thread on each method call, rather than capturing one instance permanently at startup.

questions.question: What is Spring Boot Actuator used for?
questions.answer: Spring Boot Actuator adds production-ready monitoring and management endpoints to an application with almost no code - just add the spring-boot-starter-actuator dependency. It exposes operational information about the running app over HTTP (and JMX): health status (/actuator/health), application metrics like JVM memory, GC, and HTTP request timings (/actuator/metrics), general app info (/actuator/info), configured beans (/actuator/beans), environment properties (/actuator/env), thread dumps (/actuator/threaddump), and more. These endpoints integrate naturally with monitoring stacks like Prometheus/Grafana and with orchestrators like Kubernetes, which poll /actuator/health for liveness/readiness. By default only health and info are exposed over HTTP; other endpoints must be explicitly opted into via management.endpoints.web.exposure.include, and sensitive endpoints should be secured (e.g., restricted to an ADMIN role) rather than left open in production.

questions.question: What is the Spring IoC container, and what is the difference between BeanFactory and ApplicationContext?
questions.answer: The IoC (Inversion of Control) container is the core of Spring: it's the runtime component responsible for instantiating, configuring, wiring together, and managing the lifecycle of application objects (beans), based on configuration metadata (annotations, Java config, or XML). BeanFactory is the root, most basic container interface - it provides bean instantiation and dependency wiring but is lazy by default (beans are created on first request) and lacks many enterprise conveniences. ApplicationContext is a sub-interface that extends BeanFactory with additional capabilities commonly needed in real applications: eager singleton instantiation at startup (so configuration errors surface immediately rather than at first use), event publication (ApplicationEventPublisher), internationalization support (MessageSource), and easier integration with AOP. In practice, virtually every Spring and Spring Boot application uses an ApplicationContext implementation (e.g., AnnotationConfigApplicationContext or the auto-configured one Spring Boot builds via SpringApplication.run()) rather than a raw BeanFactory.

questions.question: How does Spring Boot's auto-configuration mechanism work internally?
questions.answer: Auto-configuration is triggered by @EnableAutoConfiguration (pulled in via @SpringBootApplication). At startup, Spring Boot's AutoConfigurationImportSelector locates candidate auto-configuration classes - in modern Spring Boot these are listed in a META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports file inside each auto-configure jar (older versions used spring.factories). Each candidate is a regular @Configuration class guarded by conditional annotations: @ConditionalOnClass (only applies if a given class is on the classpath - e.g., only configure a DataSource if a JDBC driver is present), @ConditionalOnMissingBean (backs off if the user has already defined their own bean of that type - this is what makes auto-configuration 'non-invasive'), @ConditionalOnProperty (only applies if a property is set to a given value), and others. Auto-configuration is always applied after user-defined beans are registered, so a custom @Bean always wins over the auto-configured default. For example, if HikariCP and a JDBC driver are on the classpath and no DataSource bean exists, DataSourceAutoConfiguration creates a HikariDataSource with sensible defaults; define your own DataSource bean and that auto-configuration silently backs off. You can see exactly which auto-configurations were applied or excluded by starting the app with - debug, which prints a conditions evaluation report.

questions.question: Why is constructor injection generally preferred over field injection?
questions.answer: Constructor injection lets you declare dependencies as `private final` fields, which gives you true immutability and guarantees the object can never exist in a partially-wired state - if a required dependency is missing, the application fails fast at context-startup time with a clear error, rather than failing later with a NullPointerException at runtime. It also makes classes trivially unit-testable without a Spring container at all: you just call `new MyService(mockRepo)` in a plain JUnit test. Field injection (@Autowired directly on a field) is more concise but hides a class's real dependencies (you can't tell what it needs without reading every field), prevents the field from being final, silently allows circular dependencies that constructor injection would surface immediately as a startup failure, and forces you to use reflection-based tricks to inject mocks in tests. Because of these trade-offs, Spring's own team and most style guides (and tools like IntelliJ's inspections) recommend constructor injection as the default, with setter injection reserved for genuinely optional dependencies.

questions.question: What is the difference between @Primary and @Qualifier, and what happens if neither is used when multiple candidate beans exist?
questions.answer: When Spring finds more than one bean of the same type eligible for autowiring and you haven't disambiguated, it throws a NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException at startup. @Primary marks one implementation as the default choice among the candidates - if you have three NotificationService implementations, marking one @Primary means an unqualified @Autowired NotificationService injection point resolves to it automatically. @Qualifier lets you be explicit at the injection point about exactly which named bean you want (@Qualifier("smsService")), which takes precedence and is the right tool when there's no sensible 'default' and the caller genuinely needs to choose. A third, often-overlooked option is to inject a List<NotificationService> (or Map<String, NotificationService>) to get all implementations at once, useful for strategy-pattern-style dispatch. Rule of thumb: use @Primary when one implementation is clearly the sane default; use @Qualifier when the caller must pick.

questions.question: What is the order of precedence when a property is defined in multiple places (command-line args, environment variables, application.yml, profile-specific files)?
questions.answer: Spring Boot resolves the same property across many possible sources using a fixed, documented order, with later/higher-priority sources overriding earlier ones. In practical terms - from highest to lowest priority - the order most interview answers focus on is: (1) command-line arguments (--server.port=9000), (2) properties from SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON, (3) JVM system properties (-Dserver.port=9000), (4) OS environment variables, (5) profile-specific application-{profile}.properties/yml files outside the packaged jar, (6) profile-specific files inside the jar, (7) application.properties/yml outside the jar, (8) application.properties/yml packaged inside the jar, and (9) @PropertySource-annotated values and default properties set via SpringApplication.setDefaultProperties(). The official documentation lists an even more granular order that also includes things like ServletConfig/ServletContext init params, JNDI attributes, and test-specific sources (@TestPropertySource, @DynamicPropertySource) which sit above regular config files but below command-line args in priority. A practical consequence: an environment variable set in a container will silently override a value baked into application.yml, which is exactly the mechanism used to inject secrets and per-environment config without rebuilding the jar. The Actuator env and configprops endpoints are the fastest way to diagnose 'why does this property have this value' in a running app.

questions.question: What is the difference between @Value and @ConfigurationProperties, and when would you use each?
questions.answer: @Value("${some.property}") injects a single property value directly into a field via SpEL-based expression evaluation - it's quick for one-off, simple values but gets unwieldy fast: no relaxed binding rules for nested/hierarchical config, no built-in validation, and typos in the property key just silently fail (or throw at startup only if there's no default and the placeholder can't resolve) without any centralized place to see what your app actually configures. @ConfigurationProperties binds a whole block of hierarchical configuration to a strongly-typed POJO (or, in modern Spring Boot, an immutable Java record via constructor binding) - e.g., all my.service.* properties bind onto a MyProperties class with nested objects for nested prefixes. It supports relaxed binding (kebab-case, camelCase, UPPER_CASE env vars all map to the same property), can be validated with JSR-303 annotations (@Validated + @NotNull etc.), and can generate IDE auto-completion metadata. The general guidance from the Spring team itself: use @ConfigurationProperties for any group of related settings, and reserve @Value for isolated one-off values or SpEL expressions that don't fit the structured-properties model.

questions.question: How do Spring profiles work, and how do you activate one?
questions.answer: Profiles let you scope beans and configuration to specific environments (dev, test, prod, etc.). You mark a bean or @Configuration class with @Profile("dev") so it's only registered when that profile is active, and you supply profile-specific configuration files named application-{profile}.properties/yml (e.g., application-prod.yml) that Spring Boot loads in addition to the base application.yml - profile-specific values override the non-specific ones for the same key. You activate a profile by setting spring.profiles.active (a comma-separated list for multiple profiles) via a command-line arg (--spring.profiles.active=prod), an environment variable (SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod), or a system property. If several profiles are active and both define the same property, a 'last wins' strategy applies based on the order they were declared. If no profile is set explicitly, Spring Boot falls back to the implicit default profile and loads application-default.{properties|yml} if present. A subtle interview point: activating profiles via a JVM system property (-D) actually takes precedence over the same setting via an OS environment variable in current Spring Boot, which surprises people who assume it follows the general documented precedence order exactly.

questions.question: Explain the Spring bean lifecycle, and where @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy fit in.
questions.answer: A singleton bean's lifecycle inside the container roughly follows: (1) the bean definition is loaded and the container instantiates the bean (calling its constructor, which is where constructor-injected dependencies are supplied), (2) the container performs dependency injection for setter/field-injected properties, (3) if the bean implements *Aware interfaces (BeanNameAware, ApplicationContextAware, etc.), those callbacks fire, (4) BeanPostProcessors run their postProcessBeforeInitialization hook, (5) any method annotated @PostConstruct runs (and/or InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet(), and/or a custom init-method), (6) BeanPostProcessors run postProcessAfterInitialization - this is where proxies like the ones used for @Transactional and @Cacheable actually get created, wrapping the raw bean, (7) the bean is now fully initialized and ready for use for the lifetime of the application context, and finally (8) on context shutdown, any @PreDestroy method runs (and/or DisposableBean.destroy(), and/or a custom destroy-method) to release resources like closing connections or thread pools. @PostConstruct is commonly used for validating injected config or warming up caches after all dependencies are set; @PreDestroy is used for graceful cleanup (e.g., flushing buffers, closing a custom connection). Both come from the jakarta.annotation package, not Spring itself.

questions.question: What is the N+1 select problem in JPA, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: The N+1 problem happens when fetching a collection of N parent entities triggers one query for the parents and then one additional query per parent to lazily load an associated relationship - 1 query for 100 orders plus 100 more queries for each order's customer, for example, is 101 queries where 1 or 2 would suffice. It's caused by JPA/Hibernate's default lazy-loading behavior on @OneToMany and @ManyToMany associations (and can also occur with eager @ManyToOne relationships accessed in a loop). Fixes: (1) JOIN FETCH in a JPQL query (SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.customer) forces the association to load in the same single query; (2) Spring Data's @EntityGraph annotation on a repository method declaratively specifies which associations to eagerly fetch for that specific query without changing the entity's default fetch type globally, which is more reusable than scattering JOIN FETCH everywhere; (3) Hibernate batch fetching (@BatchSize or hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size) groups the N follow-up queries into a handful of IN (...) queries instead of eliminating them entirely - useful when JOIN FETCH would produce a Cartesian product across multiple collections. The problem is often invisible in development with small datasets and only shows up as a production performance issue, so many teams add a query-count assertion in tests (e.g., via a Hibernate statistics listener) to catch regressions early.

questions.question: What does @Transactional do, and why doesn't it work when a method calls another @Transactional method on this?
questions.answer: @Transactional tells Spring to wrap a method call in a database transaction: begin a transaction before the method runs, commit it if the method completes normally, and roll it back if an unchecked (RuntimeException) exception propagates out (checked exceptions do NOT trigger rollback by default unless you configure rollbackFor). Spring implements this declaratively via AOP proxies: at startup, for any bean containing @Transactional methods, Spring creates a proxy (a JDK dynamic proxy if the bean implements an interface, or a CGLIB subclass proxy otherwise) that wraps the real bean. When an external caller invokes a method on the injected bean, it's actually calling the proxy, which opens/manages the transaction and then delegates to the real method. The catch: if a method on the same class calls another @Transactional method using `this.otherMethod()`, that call goes directly to the real object, completely bypassing the proxy - so no new transaction is started or joined, and the annotation is silently ignored. This is the single most common reason @Transactional 'doesn't work' in practice. The fix is to move the inner method to a separate Spring-managed bean and inject it, or (less cleanly) inject a self-reference to the proxy (e.g., via ApplicationContext.getBean(this.getClass()) or AopContext.currentProxy() with exposeProxy=true) and call through that instead.

questions.question: How do you handle exceptions globally in a Spring Boot REST API?
questions.answer: The standard approach is a class annotated @RestControllerAdvice (or @ControllerAdvice + @ResponseBody) containing one or more @ExceptionHandler methods, which intercepts exceptions thrown from any @RestController in the application and converts them into a consistent error response instead of letting the default Whitelabel Error Page or a raw stack trace leak out. You typically write handlers for specific exception types (e.g., a custom ResourceNotFoundException mapped to 404, a MethodArgumentNotValidException from failed @Valid validation mapped to 400 with field-level error details) and a catch-all handler for generic Exception mapped to 500. Modern Spring (6+/Spring Boot 3+) encourages returning a standardized ProblemDetail object (RFC 7807 'problem+json') from these handlers, which gives a consistent JSON shape (type, title, status, detail, instance) across every error response without hand-rolling your own error DTO. A common design mistake is putting try/catch blocks in every controller method instead of centralizing error handling - @RestControllerAdvice keeps controllers focused purely on the happy path.

questions.question: What is the difference between CrudRepository and JpaRepository?
questions.answer: Both are part of the Spring Data repository interface hierarchy, and JpaRepository extends PagingAndSortingRepository, which in turn extends CrudRepository - so JpaRepository is a strict superset of CrudRepository's functionality. CrudRepository gives you the basics: save(), findById(), findAll(), deleteById(), count(), and existsById(). JpaRepository adds JPA-specific and more convenient methods on top: findAll(Sort sort) and findAll(Pageable pageable) for sorting/pagination (technically inherited via PagingAndSortingRepository), plus JPA-specific extras like saveAndFlush() (persist and immediately flush to the database rather than waiting for the transaction/session flush), deleteInBatch()/deleteAllInBatch() for more efficient bulk deletes, and getReferenceById() (formerly getOne()) for obtaining a lazy proxy reference without hitting the database. In practice, almost everyone extends JpaRepository by default in a Spring Boot + JPA app because pagination and batch operations are needed often enough that there's little reason to start with the more limited CrudRepository.

questions.question: How do you validate request bodies in a Spring Boot REST controller?
questions.answer: You annotate the request body parameter with @Valid (or @Validated for group validation) in the controller method signature, and annotate the fields of the DTO class with Jakarta Bean Validation constraints such as @NotNull, @NotBlank, @Size(min=, max=), @Email, @Min/@Max, or a custom constraint annotation. When the incoming JSON is deserialized into that DTO, Spring MVC automatically triggers validation before the handler method body runs; if any constraint fails, it throws a MethodArgumentNotValidException, which by default results in a 400 Bad Request. To return useful, field-level error messages instead of a generic 400, you write an @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class) in a @RestControllerAdvice that extracts the individual field errors from the exception's BindingResult and returns them in a structured response (or a ProblemDetail with extension fields, in modern Spring). Nested objects need @Valid on the nested field itself for validation to cascade into them, and requires the spring-boot-starter-validation dependency (Bean Validation isn't included by default in spring-boot-starter-web since Spring Boot 2.3).

questions.question: What are Spring Boot test slices such as @WebMvcTest and @DataJpaTest, and how do they differ from @SpringBootTest?
questions.answer: @SpringBootTest boots the entire Spring application context - every bean, every auto-configuration - which gives the highest confidence but is slow and pulls in dependencies (like a real web server or database, unless mocked/replaced) that aren't relevant to the specific thing you're testing. Test slices instead load only the subset of auto-configuration relevant to one architectural layer, which is faster and more focused. @WebMvcTest(MyController.class) loads only the Spring MVC infrastructure (controllers, filters, converters, a MockMvc instance for issuing simulated HTTP requests) without starting a real server or wiring up the full service/repository layers - you typically pair it with @MockBean to stub out the service layer the controller depends on. @DataJpaTest loads only JPA-related configuration (an in-memory database by default, your @Entity classes, and Spring Data repositories) with each test wrapped in a transaction that's rolled back afterward, letting you verify repository query methods against a real (embedded) database without touching the rest of the app. Other slices follow the same pattern: @JsonTest, @WebFluxTest, @RestClientTest, etc. The general strategy layered testing pyramid is: fast unit tests with plain Mockito for business logic, test slices for verifying a single layer's wiring, and a smaller number of full @SpringBootTest integration tests (often paired with Testcontainers for a real database) to verify the whole stack works together.

questions.question: How do you handle CORS in a Spring Boot application, especially when Spring Security is involved?
questions.answer: For plain Spring MVC, you can allow cross-origin requests either per-controller/method with @CrossOrigin(origins = "https://example.com") or globally by implementing WebMvcConfigurer and overriding addCorsMappings to define allowed origins, methods, and headers application-wide - this is the cleaner approach for anything beyond a single endpoint. The critical gotcha appears when Spring Security is on the classpath: Security's filter chain runs before the MVC-level CORS configuration even gets a chance to add the right response headers, so browsers' CORS preflight (OPTIONS) requests can get rejected by the security filter chain before your @CrossOrigin annotation is ever consulted. The fix is to explicitly enable CORS support inside the SecurityFilterChain configuration by calling http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults()) (which tells Security to defer to a registered CorsConfigurationSource bean) and to define that CorsConfigurationSource bean yourself with the allowed origins/methods/headers - Spring Security will not pick up @CrossOrigin or a WebMvcConfigurer's CORS mapping on its own once you have your own SecurityFilterChain in place.

questions.question: Which Actuator endpoints are exposed over HTTP by default, and how do you expose more?
questions.answer: Out of the box, Spring Boot Actuator only exposes health and info over HTTP by default - everything else (metrics, env, beans, configprops, loggers, threaddump, heapdump, etc.) is registered internally but not web-accessible until you opt in, precisely to avoid accidentally leaking sensitive application internals in production. You expose additional endpoints via management.endpoints.web.exposure.include, either a comma-separated allowlist (management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,metrics,info) or a wildcard for everything (management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*, generally discouraged in production). You can also explicitly exclude specific ones with management.endpoints.web.exposure.exclude even when using the wildcard. Because endpoints like env or heapdump can expose secrets or memory contents, best practice is to expose only what you need and put the /actuator/ path behind Spring Security (e.g., permit health/info publicly for Kubernetes probes but require an ADMIN role for everything else), and consider moving Actuator to a separate management port (management.server.port) that isn't publicly routable at all.

questions.question: Explain how Spring resolves circular dependencies between singleton beans, and why a constructor-based circular dependency cannot be resolved the same way.
questions.answer: For singleton beans wired via setter or field injection, Spring can resolve a circular dependency (Bean A needs Bean B, Bean B needs Bean A) using a three-level cache mechanism: singletonObjects (level 1, fully initialized beans), earlySingletonObjects (level 2, early references to beans that are still being constructed), and singletonFactories (level 3, ObjectFactory instances that can produce an 'early' reference to a bean-in-progress, including proxies if needed for AOP). The sequence: Spring starts creating Bean A, instantiates it (constructor runs, but properties aren't set yet), and immediately exposes a factory for A in the level-3 cache before populating its properties. When A's field/setter needs B, Spring starts creating B; B's constructor needs A, so Spring checks the caches, finds A's factory in level 3, generates an early reference to A (moving it to level 2), and injects that into B. B finishes construction, is returned and injected into A, and A completes. This works because field/setter injection allows the object to exist in a partially-constructed state that can be handed out early. Constructor injection cannot use this trick: since A's constructor itself requires a fully-formed B (and vice versa), there is no valid order to call either constructor first - Spring correctly detects this and throws BeanCurrentlyInCreationException at startup, forcing you to redesign (e.g., break the cycle with @Lazy on one of the dependencies, refactor shared logic into a third bean, or use setter injection). Note also that as of Spring Boot 2.6, circular references (even the resolvable field/setter kind) are disallowed by default; you'd need to explicitly set spring.main.allow-circular-references=true to restore the old permissive behavior, though the better fix is almost always to eliminate the cycle.

questions.question: WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter has been removed from Spring Security. How do you configure a security filter chain in a modern Spring Boot 3.x application?
questions.answer: WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter was deprecated in Spring Security 5.7 and fully removed in Spring Security 6 (which ships with Spring Boot 3), in favor of a component-based configuration style. Instead of extending an adapter class and overriding configure(HttpSecurity http), you now declare a @Bean of type SecurityFilterChain inside a @Configuration class (@EnableWebSecurity is technically no longer strictly required but is still commonly used for clarity), and build the chain with a lambda-DSL style: http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.requestMatchers("/public/").permitAll().anyRequest().authenticated()).httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults()); return http.build();. Several supporting APIs changed alongside this: authorizeRequests() became authorizeHttpRequests(); and the old antMatchers()/mvcMatchers()/regexMatchers() were all consolidated into a single requestMatchers() method. Multiple SecurityFilterChain beans can coexist (ordered via @Order) to apply different rules to different URL patterns - e.g., a stateless, JWT-based chain for /api/ and a stateful, form-login chain for the rest of the app. This component-based style is more testable and composable than the old inheritance-based adapter, since each concern (authorization rules, authentication mechanism, CSRF, CORS) is configured explicitly on the HttpSecurity object rather than hidden inside overridden protected methods.

questions.question: How would you diagnose and fix a slow-starting Spring Boot application?
questions.answer: First, quantify where the time actually goes rather than guessing - start the app with - debug to get the auto-configuration conditions report, and enable the Actuator startup endpoint (management.endpoint.startup.enabled=true, backed by ApplicationStartup/BufferingApplicationStartup) or use spring-boot-starter-actuator's startup timeline to see which beans and auto-configurations take the longest during context refresh. Common root causes and fixes: (1) Excessive component scanning - a @ComponentScan with too broad a base package, or too many classpath JARs scanned for annotations; narrow the scan or use explicit @Import where possible. (2) Heavy eager singleton initialization - e.g., beans doing expensive work (network calls, large cache warm-up) in their constructor or @PostConstruct; defer that work to a background task or make the bean lazy with @Lazy. (3) Too many auto-configurations being evaluated - excluding unused ones (spring.autoconfigure.exclude) trims unnecessary condition evaluation. (4) JPA/Hibernate metamodel building and JDBC connection pool warm-up can be slow for large schemas; consider deferring datasource initialization or tuning HikariCP's initial pool size. (5) Classpath scanning overhead from too many JARs on the classpath - modularizing dependencies helps. For applications where startup time is critical (serverless, frequent scale-to-zero, CLI tools), the more structural fixes are Spring's AOT (Ahead-of-Time) processing introduced in Spring Boot 3, which pre-computes much of the bean-definition/auto-configuration work at build time instead of at runtime, and ultimately compiling to a GraalVM native image, which eliminates JVM class-loading and reflection-based startup cost almost entirely (startup drops from seconds to tens of milliseconds).

questions.question: What is the open-session-in-view (OSIV) pattern in Spring Boot, and why might you want to disable it in production?
questions.answer: OSIV keeps a Hibernate Session (JPA persistence context) open for the entire duration of an HTTP request, not just for the duration of the @Transactional service method. It's implemented via a servlet filter/interceptor that opens the session at the start of the request and closes it after the view has been rendered (or the response body serialized). Spring Boot enables OSIV by default and logs a warning about it at startup precisely because it's controversial. The upside is developer convenience: lazily-loaded associations can still be navigated later in the request (e.g., while Jackson is serializing the response, or in a Thymeleaf template) without throwing a LazyInitializationException, even though the original @Transactional method has already returned and committed. The downsides, which is why many teams explicitly disable it (spring.jpa.open-in-view=false): (1) it hides where actual database queries happen - a getter call deep in your serialization layer can silently trigger a query, making the true query pattern (and N+1 problems) hard to see, since those extra queries run outside the original transaction and in auto-commit mode, adding extra load per statement; (2) more importantly, it holds a database connection borrowed from the pool for the entire request lifecycle, including any time spent waiting on slow, unrelated I/O like an external HTTP call - under load, this can exhaust the connection pool and make the whole application unresponsive even though the actual database work is fast. Disabling OSIV forces you to be intentional about fetching everything you need inside the transactional method (via JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or DTO projections), trading some convenience for predictable, bounded connection usage and clearer query behavior.

questions.question: How do you implement a circuit breaker in a Spring Boot microservice, and what states does it transition through?
questions.answer: The standard implementation is Resilience4j (via spring-cloud-starter-circuitbreaker-resilience4j or resilience4j-spring-boot3), applied with a @CircuitBreaker(name = "inventoryService", fallbackMethod = "fallback") annotation around a method that calls a potentially unreliable downstream service, plus a fallback method with a matching signature (plus a Throwable parameter) that returns a degraded response instead of propagating the failure. Configuration (in application.yml under resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.*) controls the sliding window type (count-based or time-based), the failure-rate threshold that trips the breaker, the wait duration in the open state, and how many trial calls are permitted in half-open. The circuit breaker is a finite state machine with three normal states: CLOSED (the default - all calls pass through and failures/successes are recorded in a sliding window; if the failure rate crosses the configured threshold, it trips to OPEN), OPEN (calls are rejected immediately without even attempting the downstream call - this 'fails fast' and protects the caller's threads/resources from piling up waiting on a struggling dependency; after a configured wait duration it moves to HALF_OPEN), and HALF_OPEN (a limited number of trial calls are let through to test whether the dependency has recovered - if they succeed, the breaker returns to CLOSED; if they fail, it goes back to OPEN). Resilience4j also defines two special states - DISABLED (bypasses the breaker entirely) and FORCED_OPEN (manually forces rejection, useful for planned maintenance) - that can be set programmatically. In practice, circuit breakers are usually combined with other resilience patterns: a Retry for transient failures, a Bulkhead to cap concurrent calls to a dependency, and a TimeLimiter to bound how long a call is allowed to take, since a hanging call that never fails or succeeds can defeat the circuit breaker entirely.

questions.question: How do you achieve data consistency across microservices without distributed transactions (e.g., the Saga pattern, transactional outbox)?
questions.answer: Classic two-phase-commit distributed transactions don't scale well across independently-deployed microservices with separate databases (they require all participants to be available and lock resources for the duration, killing availability and throughput). The Saga pattern replaces one big atomic transaction with a sequence of local transactions, each in its own service, where each step publishes an event/message that triggers the next step; if a step fails, previously completed steps are undone via explicit compensating transactions (e.g., if payment fails after inventory was reserved, publish a 'release inventory' compensating action) rather than a database-level rollback. Sagas are coordinated either choreography-style (each service reacts to events from the previous one, with no central coordinator - simpler but harder to trace/debug as the number of steps grows) or orchestration-style (a central saga orchestrator explicitly tells each service what to do next and handles failure/compensation logic - easier to reason about and test, at the cost of a new coordinating component). A closely related and commonly paired pattern is the transactional outbox: instead of a service updating its own database and then separately publishing a message to Kafka/RabbitMQ (which is not atomic - a crash between the two leaves them inconsistent), the service writes both the business change and the outgoing event/message to an 'outbox' table in the same local database transaction; a separate poller or change-data-capture process (e.g., Debezium) then reliably relays outbox rows to the message broker, guaranteeing the state change and the event are never out of sync. Together, Sagas and the outbox pattern give you eventual consistency across services without any distributed lock or two-phase commit, at the cost of accepting that the system is only consistent 'eventually', not instantaneously - which has real implications for what your APIs can promise to callers in the interim.

questions.question: How do virtual threads change how a Spring Boot MVC application scales under load, and what are the caveats?
questions.answer: Traditional Spring MVC uses a thread-per-request model backed by a bounded platform-thread pool (Tomcat's default is around 200 threads); when a request blocks on I/O (a JDBC call, an outbound HTTP call), that expensive OS thread sits idle waiting, and once all pool threads are occupied, new requests queue up - this is exactly the scaling problem that pushed some teams toward Spring WebFlux's non-blocking reactive model. Java 21's virtual threads (Project Loom) offer a middle path: they're extremely lightweight, JVM-managed threads that can number in the hundreds of thousands, and when a virtual thread blocks on I/O, the underlying platform ('carrier') thread is released to run other virtual threads instead of sitting idle - so you keep writing simple, blocking, imperative code (JDBC, RestTemplate/RestClient, synchronized blocks with caveats) but get much of reactive's scalability under I/O-bound load. Spring Boot 3.2+ added first-class support: setting spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true switches the embedded Tomcat's request-handling threads (and @Async executors) to virtual threads with no code changes to your controllers. The caveats matter for an interview answer: virtual threads only help for I/O-bound blocking work - they don't speed up CPU-bound work at all; 'pinning' can occur when a virtual thread executes inside a synchronized block or a native method while blocked, which prevents the carrier thread from being released and can reintroduce the scaling bottleneck you were trying to escape (this has improved across recent JDK versions but is still worth knowing); connection pools (like HikariCP) sized for a small platform-thread pool may need re-tuning since virtual threads can now issue far more concurrent blocking calls than before, potentially overwhelming a downstream database or service that wasn't designed for that concurrency; and virtual threads don't replace WebFlux for genuinely reactive, backpressure-aware streaming scenarios - they're a scalability upgrade for the traditional blocking programming model, not a full substitute for reactive semantics.

questions.question: What are GraalVM native images in Spring Boot, and what trade-offs come with using them?
questions.answer: A GraalVM native image ahead-of-time (AOT) compiles a Spring Boot application into a standalone, platform-specific executable that includes a minimal runtime, rather than shipping bytecode that a JVM interprets/JIT-compiles at startup. Spring Boot 3 added first-class support for this via Spring's AOT engine, which pre-computes bean definitions, proxy classes, and reflection/resource configuration at build time (since GraalVM's closed-world assumption means it can't discover new classes via reflection at runtime the way a normal JVM can) - you build it with the native-image Maven/Gradle plugin goal, typically via GraalVM's own compiler or Cloud Native Buildpacks so you don't need GraalVM installed locally. The main benefit is startup time and memory footprint: native images typically start in tens of milliseconds instead of seconds, and use a fraction of the memory of a running JVM, which matters enormously for serverless/FaaS platforms (cold starts), scale-to-zero container workloads, and CLI tools. The trade-offs are real: build times are dramatically longer (minutes instead of seconds, since the whole app is compiled ahead of time) and more resource-intensive; peak throughput after warm-up is generally lower than a long-running JIT-compiled JVM, because the JIT can perform runtime profile-guided optimizations that AOT compilation can't; reflection, dynamic proxies, and classpath resource loading that aren't already covered by Spring's AOT processing need explicit reachability-metadata hints, so third-party libraries that rely heavily on runtime reflection (an old ORM plugin, some dynamic serialization libraries) may not work out of the box and need extra configuration or aren't natively supported at all; and debugging/profiling tooling for native images is less mature than the standard JVM ecosystem. The practical guidance: native images shine for short-lived processes and latency-sensitive cold-start scenarios; a normal JVM deployment is usually still the better default for long-running, high-throughput services where startup time isn't the bottleneck.

questions.question: How would you use Testcontainers to run integration tests against a real database instead of an in-memory database like H2?
questions.answer: Testcontainers spins up real, disposable Docker containers (a real PostgreSQL, MySQL, Kafka, Redis, etc.) for the duration of a test run, giving you integration tests that exercise the actual database engine your application uses in production - this matters because H2's SQL dialect, constraint behavior, and locking semantics can diverge from a real production database in ways that hide bugs (a query that works fine against H2's SQL-mode emulation of Postgres can fail against real Postgres). In a Spring Boot 3.1+ project you add the spring-boot-testcontainers dependency and either annotate a @Bean method with @ServiceConnection returning a container instance (Spring Boot auto-detects the container type and wires up the corresponding DataSource/connection properties automatically, no manual property overriding needed), or use @Testcontainers + @Container on a static container field plus @DynamicPropertySource to manually register the container's JDBC URL/credentials into the Spring Environment before the context starts. The container's lifecycle can be scoped per test class (each test class gets a fresh container, slower but fully isolated) or shared across the whole suite via a singleton container pattern (a static container reused across test classes for speed, common when spinning up the same Postgres/Kafka image repeatedly would otherwise dominate the test run's wall-clock time). This pattern is typically combined with @SpringBootTest for full-stack integration tests, and is now the de facto standard for testing anything that touches a real datastore, message broker, or third-party service that has an official Testcontainers module, since it gives production-fidelity tests that are still fully reproducible and don't require a shared, stateful test database.

questions.question: Explain transaction propagation and isolation levels in Spring, and describe a scenario where the propagation setting matters.
questions.answer: Propagation controls how a @Transactional method's transaction relates to an already-in-progress transaction when one method calls another. The default, REQUIRED, joins the caller's existing transaction if there is one, or starts a new one if there isn't - this is right for most business logic that should live or die with its caller. REQUIRES_NEW always suspends any current transaction and starts a fresh, independent one, which commits or rolls back on its own regardless of what happens to the outer transaction afterward - this is the setting that actually matters in a concrete scenario: imagine placeOrder() saves an order and then calls auditService.logActivity(), and you want the audit log entry to persist even if the order save later fails and the outer transaction rolls back (or conversely, you want a failure in the audit call to not roll back a successful order). Marking logActivity() as REQUIRES_NEW gives it its own commit/rollback boundary, completely decoupled from the caller's transaction outcome. Other propagation types: SUPPORTS (join if a transaction exists, otherwise run non-transactionally), MANDATORY (must run inside an existing transaction, throws if none exists), NOT_SUPPORTED (suspends any existing transaction and runs without one), NEVER (throws if a transaction exists), and NESTED (runs within a savepoint of the current transaction if one exists - a partial rollback to that savepoint is possible without rolling back the entire outer transaction, though this is only supported by specific transaction managers like DataSourceTransactionManager and has caveats under JpaTransactionManager). Isolation, in contrast, controls how much a transaction can see of concurrent, uncommitted changes made by other transactions - it's one of the four ACID properties. Spring exposes the standard JDBC isolation levels: READ_UNCOMMITTED (weakest - allows dirty reads), READ_COMMITTED (a common default - prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads), REPEATABLE_READ (prevents dirty and non-repeatable reads but allows phantom reads), and SERIALIZABLE (strongest - fully isolates concurrent transactions as if run sequentially, at the cost of the most locking/lowest concurrency). By default, Spring uses Isolation.DEFAULT, meaning whatever the underlying database's default is (commonly READ_COMMITTED for Postgres/Oracle, REPEATABLE_READ for MySQL/InnoDB), and it's rarely overridden except for specific correctness-critical operations (e.g., using SERIALIZABLE briefly around a balance-check-then-debit sequence in a financial system) because higher isolation levels increase lock contention and the risk of deadlocks under load.

questions.question: What is the difference between @PathVariable and @RequestParam in a Spring Boot REST controller?
questions.answer: @PathVariable extracts a value from a segment of the URI path itself - e.g., in @GetMapping("/users/{id}") public User getUser(@PathVariable Long id), the id comes from the path (/users/42). @RequestParam extracts a value from the query string (?key=value) or from form data in a request - e.g., @GetMapping("/users") public List<User> search(@RequestParam(required = false) String name) reads ?name=Alice from /users?name=Alice. The distinction maps to how you design the URL: path variables identify a specific resource (a resource's identity is part of the URL path, as in REST conventions), while request parameters are used for filtering, optional criteria, sorting, or pagination on a collection endpoint. Both support type conversion (Spring converts the String from the URL/query into the target type like Long, LocalDate, or an enum) and both can be marked required=false (or given a defaultValue) for optional parameters - @PathVariable, however, is inherently required by definition since it's part of the URL template that must match for the route to resolve at all.

questions.question: How do you enable caching in a Spring Boot application, and what does @Cacheable do?
questions.answer: You add the spring-boot-starter-cache dependency and annotate a @Configuration class (or the main application class) with @EnableCaching, which activates Spring's caching AOP infrastructure. By default, Spring Boot falls back to a simple in-memory ConcurrentHashMap-based cache if no CacheManager bean and no caching library (Caffeine, EhCache, Redis, Hazelcast) is on the classpath - fine for local testing but not suitable for production, since it isn't bounded, evicted, or shared across instances. @Cacheable("products") on a method tells Spring: before running this method, check whether a result for these arguments already exists in the named cache; if so, return the cached value and skip the method body entirely; if not, run the method, store the result in the cache, and return it. Internally this works the same way as @Transactional - via an AOP proxy that intercepts the call - so it has the same self-invocation limitation (calling the method via `this` inside the same class bypasses caching). A common production setup pairs @Cacheable with an explicit CacheManager bean (e.g., Caffeine with maximumSize and expireAfterWrite) since the default cache never evicts entries and can grow unbounded.

questions.question: What is the @Scheduled annotation used for, and what do you need to enable before it works?
questions.answer: @Scheduled marks a method to be run automatically and repeatedly by Spring's task scheduler, without any external trigger like an HTTP request. You configure the timing via one of its attributes: fixedRate = 5000 (run every 5 seconds, measured from the start of the previous execution), fixedDelay = 5000 (run 5 seconds after the previous execution finishes), initialDelay (wait before the first run), or cron = "0 0 * *" for full cron-expression-based scheduling (e.g., 'every day at 2am'). Before any @Scheduled method will actually run, you must add @EnableScheduling to a @Configuration class (typically the main application class) - without it, Spring simply ignores the annotation and the method never executes; this is a very common gotcha for people new to the annotation. A separate but related gotcha: by default all @Scheduled methods run on a single shared thread, so one long-running or blocking scheduled task delays every other scheduled task - for real workloads you typically configure a dedicated TaskScheduler bean with a larger thread pool.

questions.question: What is Spring Boot DevTools, and what development problem does it solve?
questions.answer: Spring Boot DevTools (spring-boot-devtools, scope=runtime, and marked optional so it doesn't get bundled into production artifacts) speeds up the local development feedback loop. Its core feature is automatic restart: it monitors the classpath, and whenever a class file changes (e.g., you recompile after editing code in your IDE), it triggers a fast application restart automatically instead of you manually stopping and re-running the app. It's fast because DevTools uses two classloaders - a 'base' classloader for unchanging third-party JARs and a 'restart' classloader for your own application classes - so only the restart classloader needs to reload, which is much quicker than a full cold start. DevTools also disables template caching (Thymeleaf, FreeMarker, etc.) so template edits show up on refresh without a restart, and it integrates with LiveReload to auto-refresh the browser. It's automatically disabled when running a fully packaged jar (java -jar) so it never accidentally ships to production, and it's development-only tooling - it has no effect on runtime application behavior.

questions.question: What is a DTO, and why is it generally a bad idea to expose JPA entities directly from a REST API?
questions.answer: A DTO (Data Transfer Object) is a plain object whose only job is to carry data across a boundary - in this context, between your REST API's JSON representation and your internal domain/persistence model - rather than reusing your @Entity classes directly as request/response bodies. Returning entities directly from a controller causes several real problems: (1) it tightly couples your public API contract to your database schema, so a harmless internal refactor (renaming a column, adding a field, changing a relationship) becomes a breaking API change for every client; (2) lazy-loaded associations can trigger LazyInitializationException when Jackson tries to serialize them outside a transaction (or silently trigger extra N+1 queries if OSIV is enabled), and bidirectional @OneToMany/@ManyToOne relationships can cause infinite recursion during JSON serialization unless you carefully manage @JsonIgnore/@JsonManagedReference; (3) it risks leaking sensitive fields (password hashes, internal audit columns, other users' data) that exist on the entity but were never meant to be public; (4) it prevents you from shaping the response differently from the persistence model - e.g., combining fields from multiple entities, or hiding fields based on the caller's role. DTOs (often paired with a mapping library like MapStruct to avoid writing repetitive conversion code by hand) decouple 'what the database looks like' from 'what the API contract promises', which is what lets each evolve independently.

questions.question: How do you handle a file upload in a Spring Boot REST controller?
questions.answer: You accept the upload as a MultipartFile parameter in a controller method, annotated with @RequestParam("file"), and configure the endpoint to accept multipart/form-data. Before processing, you should validate the upload - check file.isEmpty(), enforce a maximum size (spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size and max-request-size in application.yml, plus a size check in code), and validate the content type/extension against an allowlist rather than trusting the client-supplied contentType. Files should be given a generated, collision-proof name (e.g., a UUID) rather than trusting the original filename directly, both to avoid path-traversal issues and filename collisions. For storage: writing directly to local disk (Files.write / Path.of("uploads").resolve(filename)) works for a single-instance app, but in any horizontally-scaled deployment you should store files in external object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob, or a shared network volume) and keep only the metadata (original name, content type, size, storage key) in your database, since local disk storage isn't shared across instances and is lost if a container is rescheduled.

questions.question: What is the purpose of spring-boot-starter-parent (or the Spring Boot BOM) in a Maven project?
questions.answer: spring-boot-starter-parent is a special Maven parent POM that gives your project sensible, centrally-managed defaults so you don't have to configure them yourself: it defines a dependencyManagement section (the actual Bill of Materials, spring-boot-dependencies) that pins compatible, tested versions for every library across the Spring Boot ecosystem and its common third-party dependencies (Jackson, JUnit, Hibernate, Tomcat, etc.), so when you declare spring-boot-starter-web with no explicit version, Maven resolves it and all its transitive dependencies to versions known to work well together. It also sets useful defaults like the Java source/target version, default resource filtering, and a pre-configured spring-boot-maven-plugin execution for building an executable jar. If you already have your own parent POM and can't extend spring-boot-starter-parent directly (common in multi-module or enterprise setups), you can still get the same version management by importing spring-boot-dependencies as a <dependencyManagement><import> scope entry instead - the goal either way is to avoid manually tracking compatible versions for dozens of interdependent libraries, which is exactly the 'dependency hell' problem Spring Boot's curated starters solve.

questions.question: How do you implement pagination and sorting in a Spring Data JPA repository?
questions.answer: If your repository extends PagingAndSortingRepository or JpaRepository, you get pagination and sorting essentially for free by adding a Pageable (or Sort) parameter to a query method - Spring Data JPA generates the LIMIT/OFFSET and ORDER BY clauses automatically. For example: Page<User> findByLastName(String lastName, Pageable pageable). In a controller, you typically accept page and size as request parameters and build a PageRequest.of(page, size, Sort.by("lastName").ascending()) to pass in; Spring MVC can also auto-resolve a Pageable method argument directly from query params (page, size, sort=field,asc) if you enable Spring Data's web support. The returned Page<T> object carries not just the current page's content but also useful metadata - totalElements, totalPages, isFirst()/isLast(), hasNext()/hasPrevious() - which the client can use to build pagination UI without a separate count query (Spring Data issues that count query internally for you). Returning paginated results instead of a full findAll() list is a standard practice for any endpoint whose collection can grow unbounded, both to protect response size/latency and to avoid loading excessive data into memory.

questions.question: What is Spring Boot's default logging framework, and how do you change the logging level for a specific package?
questions.answer: Spring Boot uses Commons Logging (spring-jcl) as the API abstraction internally, but the default logging implementation wired up by the starters is Logback, configured with sensible console output out of the box - spring-boot-starter includes spring-boot-starter-logging, which pulls in Logback plus a bridge (jcl-over-slf4j / SLF4J) so any library logging through Commons Logging, Log4j, or java.util.logging also routes through the same pipeline. To change the log level for a specific package, you set a property in application.properties/yml: logging.level.com.example.myapp=DEBUG (or logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG to see generated SQL, a common debugging technique). You can also target the root logger with logging.level.root=WARN. For anything beyond simple level tweaks - custom appenders, rolling file policies, JSON output for log aggregation - you provide your own logback-spring.xml (the -spring suffix lets you use Spring profile-specific configuration inside it), which Spring Boot picks up automatically if present on the classpath, overriding the default configuration. If you prefer Log4j2 instead, you exclude spring-boot-starter-logging and add spring-boot-starter-log4j2, since only one logging implementation should be on the classpath at a time.

questions.question: How do you add a custom health check to Spring Boot Actuator by implementing HealthIndicator?
questions.answer: You create a Spring-managed bean implementing the HealthIndicator interface (or extend AbstractHealthIndicator for a slightly more convenient base class), overriding its health() method to return a Health object built via Health.up()/.down()/.outOfService(), optionally chained with .withDetail("key", value) to attach diagnostic information. For example, a custom check that verifies a downstream payment gateway is reachable would return Health.up().withDetail("gateway", "reachable").build() on success or Health.down(exception).build() on failure. Spring Boot auto-detects any bean implementing HealthIndicator and automatically incorporates it into the aggregated result at /actuator/health - the naming convention matters: a bean named paymentGatewayHealthIndicator contributes an indicator visible as health.components.paymentGateway (the "HealthIndicator" suffix is stripped). The overall application health rolls up all indicators (built-in ones like db, diskSpace, ping, plus your custom ones) using a configurable status aggregator, where any single DOWN component typically makes the whole application report DOWN - which matters a lot if that indicator is being polled by a Kubernetes liveness or readiness probe, since a flaky non-critical dependency check can accidentally take healthy pods out of rotation.

questions.question: What is the difference between @CachePut, @CacheEvict, and @Cacheable, and when would you use each?
questions.answer: All three are part of Spring's declarative cache abstraction, but they control different lifecycle actions on a cache entry. @Cacheable checks the cache first and skips method execution entirely on a hit - use it for read/lookup methods where you want to avoid repeating expensive work (a database read, an external API call) for the same arguments. @CachePut always executes the annotated method (unlike @Cacheable, it never skips execution) and then stores the method's return value in the cache under the derived key - use it on update/write operations where you want the cache to be refreshed with the new value as a side effect of the write, keeping the cache in sync without a separate read. @CacheEvict removes one or more entries from the cache (or, with allEntries = true, clears the entire cache region) and is typically placed on delete or update operations to invalidate stale data rather than trying to overwrite it - commonly paired with @CachePut style updates, or used alone when the write path doesn't naturally produce a value worth caching. A frequent design pattern: a getProduct() method uses @Cacheable, while updateProduct() uses @CacheEvict(key = "#id") to invalidate the now-stale cached entry for that product on write, rather than trying to keep the cache perfectly current with @CachePut.

questions.question: What is method-level security in Spring Security, and how do @PreAuthorize and @PostAuthorize differ?
questions.answer: Method-level security lets you enforce authorization rules directly on individual service or controller methods (via Spring AOP proxies, same mechanism as @Transactional/@Cacheable) rather than only at the URL/endpoint level in the SecurityFilterChain, which is useful for fine-grained checks that depend on method arguments or the returned object rather than just the URL pattern. You enable it with @EnableMethodSecurity on a configuration class. @PreAuthorize evaluates a SpEL (Spring Expression Language) expression before the method executes; if it evaluates to false, Spring AOP blocks the call entirely and throws an AccessDeniedException without the method body ever running - e.g., @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") or @PreAuthorize("#userId == authentication.name") to check that the caller's own ID matches an argument. @PostAuthorize evaluates its expression after the method has already executed, and is the only one of the two that can inspect the method's return value via the returnObject variable - e.g., @PostAuthorize("returnObject.ownerUsername == authentication.name") to ensure a user can only see an entity they own, which is impossible to express with @PreAuthorize since the object being checked doesn't exist until the method runs. The trade-off: @PostAuthorize's check happens after the (potentially expensive, or side-effecting) method body has already run, so it's less efficient and unsuitable for methods with irreversible side effects that shouldn't happen if authorization fails - @PreAuthorize is preferred whenever the check can be expressed purely from the input arguments and current authentication. Like all Spring AOP-based security, both annotations only intercept public method calls and are silently bypassed by self-invocation (calling the method via `this` within the same class).

questions.question: How would you secure a REST API with JWT using Spring Security's OAuth2 resource server support?
questions.answer: In a modern (Spring Security 6 / Spring Boot 3) app, the idiomatic path is to add spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server, configure your app as an OAuth2 resource server via http.oauth2ResourceServer(oauth2 -> oauth2.jwt()) inside your SecurityFilterChain bean, and point Spring at the issuer's JWK Set (public key) endpoint via spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri (or jwk-set-uri directly) so it can verify token signatures without you writing any JWT-parsing code yourself. The overall flow: a user authenticates once against an identity provider (Keycloak, Okta, Auth0, or your own auth server), which issues a signed JWT containing the user's identity and roles/scopes as claims; the client sends this token on every subsequent request in the Authorization: Bearer <token> header; each resource-server microservice independently validates the token's signature and expiry (stateless - no session lookup, no shared session store needed) and extracts roles/scopes from its claims for authorization decisions (e.g., @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_read')") or requestMatchers(...).hasRole(...) checks against the JWT's claims). This is the standard shape used for securing microservices behind an API gateway: the gateway (or each service directly) validates the JWT as a resource server rather than every service maintaining its own session state, which is what makes the architecture horizontally scalable without sticky sessions. A key production detail: token revocation is inherently harder with stateless JWTs since there's no server-side session to invalidate - teams typically mitigate this with short token lifetimes plus refresh tokens, or a token-blocklist check for the rare cases (e.g., a password reset) requiring immediate revocation.

questions.question: What is the difference between optimistic and pessimistic locking in Spring Data JPA, and when would you choose each?
questions.answer: Both are strategies for handling concurrent updates to the same row without corrupting data, but they take opposite approaches. Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare: you add a @Version field (an int/long, or a timestamp) to your entity, and Hibernate includes it in the WHERE clause of every UPDATE (UPDATE product SET price=?, version=? WHERE id=? AND version=?). If another transaction has already updated the row (and thus bumped the version) since you read it, the WHERE clause matches zero rows, and JPA throws an OptimisticLockException - no database-level locks are held while you're just reading or thinking about the data, so throughput is high and it scales well for read-heavy workloads with occasional write conflicts. Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts are common enough to actively prevent: you use @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) (or PESSIMISTIC_READ for a shared lock) on a repository query method, which causes the database to take a real row-level lock (typically via SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) for the duration of the transaction, blocking other transactions from reading (with PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) or writing until the lock is released. The trade-off is straightforward: optimistic locking gives better concurrency/throughput but pushes conflict handling to the application layer (you must catch the exception and retry or surface an error to the user); pessimistic locking guarantees no lost updates and is simpler to reason about, but can cause blocking, reduced throughput under contention, and even deadlocks if lock acquisition order isn't consistent. Pick optimistic for typical web-app CRUD where conflicting concurrent edits on the same row are rare (e.g., two admins editing the same product listing); pick pessimistic for scenarios with frequent, high-stakes contention on the same rows, such as decrementing limited inventory stock or processing a financial ledger, where you genuinely need to serialize access rather than detect conflicts after the fact.

questions.question: How do you version a REST API in Spring Boot, and what are the trade-offs of the common approaches (URI, header, media type)?
questions.answer: The three common strategies are URI versioning (/api/v1/users, /api/v2/users - implemented as separate @RequestMapping paths, or entirely separate controller classes per version), header-based versioning (a custom header like X-API-Version: 2, matched via a custom RequestCondition or headers attribute on @GetMapping), and media-type/content-negotiation versioning (Accept: application/vnd.myapp.v2+json, matched via the produces attribute). URI versioning is the most common in practice: it's simple, self-documenting, trivially cacheable and routable at the infrastructure/gateway/CDN level since the version is visible in the URL, and easy for clients and API consumers to understand and test manually - the downside is that it technically means each version is 'a different resource' in REST terms, which purists dislike, and you can end up duplicating a lot of controller/routing logic across versions. Header-based versioning keeps URLs clean and semantically stable (the same URI always identifies 'the current user resource', just with different representations), but is less visible/discoverable, harder to test with a plain browser, and requires clients to remember to set the header correctly. Media-type versioning is the most 'RESTfully pure' (a resource's URI never changes, only its representation does), but it adds the most complexity for both server-side routing logic and client tooling, and is the least common in practice outside of API-design-purist shops. In practice, most teams pick URI versioning for its simplicity and operational visibility, and the key organizational rule regardless of strategy is consistency - pick one approach and apply it uniformly across the whole API rather than mixing strategies.

questions.question: How do you produce and consume messages in a Spring Boot application using Kafka or RabbitMQ?
questions.answer: For Kafka: add spring-kafka, configure the broker address (spring.kafka.bootstrap-servers) plus serializer/deserializer settings, inject a KafkaTemplate<K,V> and call kafkaTemplate.send(topic, key, value) to produce, and annotate a method with @KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "order-service") to consume - Spring Kafka handles polling, deserialization, and offset management under the hood, with sensible auto-commit defaults you can override for manual acknowledgment when you need at-least-once processing guarantees tied to successful business logic completion rather than just message receipt. For RabbitMQ: add spring-boot-starter-amqp, configure the connection (spring.rabbitmq.host/port/username/password), inject a RabbitTemplate and call rabbitTemplate.convertAndSend(queueName, message) to produce, and annotate a method with @RabbitListener(queues = "notificationQueue") to consume. Both integrations use Spring's message converters (typically Jackson-based for JSON) to automatically serialize/deserialize POJOs rather than dealing with raw bytes. For production reliability beyond the basic happy path, you generally need to add: retry with backoff for transient consumer failures, a dead-letter queue/topic to capture messages that repeatedly fail processing rather than looping forever, and (for Kafka specifically) awareness that delivery is at-least-once by default - consumers should be designed idempotently since redelivery after a crash or rebalance is a normal, expected occurrence rather than an edge case.

questions.question: How does Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher and @EventListener work, and when would you use application events instead of a direct method call?
questions.answer: ApplicationEventPublisher lets a bean publish an arbitrary event object (publisher.publishEvent(new OrderCreatedEvent(this, order))) without knowing or caring which beans, if any, are listening for it; any bean with a method annotated @EventListener that accepts that event type is automatically invoked by the container when the event is published - you register no explicit wiring between publisher and listener beyond the event type itself. By default, listeners run synchronously on the same thread as the publisher (the publish call blocks until every listener has finished), but you can make a specific listener asynchronous by adding @Async on it (with @EnableAsync configured), or use @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) to defer execution until the enclosing transaction has successfully committed, which is a common and important pattern - e.g., only sending a 'welcome email' or publishing an outbound message to Kafka after the order-creation transaction is guaranteed to have committed, rather than risking sending a notification for a transaction that later rolls back. The main reason to reach for events instead of a direct method call is decoupling: OrderService shouldn't need a compile-time dependency on EmailService, InventoryService, and AnalyticsService just to notify them that an order was created - it publishes one event and lets each interested module subscribe independently, so adding a new listener later requires zero changes to the publisher. The trade-off is that this indirection makes the codebase harder to trace (a debugger stepping through OrderService.createOrder() won't obviously show you every side effect that happens as a result), so it's best reserved for genuinely decoupled, optional side effects rather than core business logic steps that must always happen in a specific order as part of the same unit of work.
