questions.question: How do you build an efficient Docker image for a Spring Boot application?
questions.answer: A naive Dockerfile that just COPYs the whole fat jar and runs java -jar app.jar works but wastes layer caching: any code change invalidates the entire jar layer, forcing Docker to re-push the whole (often 50MB+) artifact even if only one class changed. The standard optimization is to use Spring Boot's layered jar support: the spring-boot-maven-plugin (or Gradle plugin) can produce a layered jar (or you extract it with java -Djarmode=layertools -jar app.jar extract), splitting it into layers such as dependencies (rarely changes), spring-boot-loader, snapshot-dependencies, and application (your own classes - changes on every build). A multi-stage Dockerfile then COPYs each layer separately, from the least-frequently-changing to the most-frequently-changing, so Docker's layer cache only needs to rebuild/repush the thin 'application' layer on a typical code change, dramatically speeding up CI/CD image builds and registry pushes. Additional efficiency practices: use a minimal base image (eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine or similar JRE-only image rather than a full JDK image, since you don't need the compiler at runtime), run as a non-root user for security, and avoid unnecessary build tools/caches ending up in the final image (a multi-stage build compiles in one stage and copies only the built artifact into a clean final stage). An alternative to hand-writing Dockerfiles entirely is Spring Boot's built-in Cloud Native Buildpacks support (mvn spring-boot:build-image), which produces an already-optimized, layered OCI image without you maintaining a Dockerfile at all.

questions.question: How do you manage session state for a Spring Boot application running behind a load balancer across multiple instances?
questions.answer: The default in-memory HTTP session (stored on whichever server instance handled the login) breaks as soon as you scale beyond one instance, since a follow-up request from the same user can land on a different instance that has no idea who they are. There are three standard fixes. (1) Stateless authentication (JWT): don't store server-side session state at all - the client holds a signed token containing the user's identity/claims, and any instance can validate it independently without shared state; this is the natural fit for REST APIs and is the most horizontally-scalable option since it requires zero coordination between instances. (2) Sticky sessions: configure the load balancer to always route a given client's requests to the same backend instance (based on a cookie or source IP), so the in-memory session on that instance is always the one consulted; this requires no code changes, but reduces the load balancer's flexibility (uneven load distribution, and a lost instance loses all sessions pinned to it) and doesn't fit well with auto-scaling. (3) A distributed/shared session store via Spring Session: session data is externalized to a shared store like Redis (spring.session.store-type=redis) or a JDBC-backed store, so any instance can read/write any user's session - this preserves traditional server-side session semantics (useful for stateful web apps using Thymeleaf/JSP rather than a pure API) while remaining horizontally scalable, at the cost of an extra network hop to the session store and the store itself becoming a piece of shared infrastructure to operate. For new REST APIs, JWT/stateless auth is generally preferred; Spring Session with Redis is the standard answer when you genuinely need server-side session state (e.g., a traditional server-rendered web app) across multiple instances.

questions.question: Why doesn't @Async take effect when a method calls another @Async method on this, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: This is exactly the same proxy self-invocation limitation that affects @Transactional, @Cacheable, and Spring Security's method annotations, and it stems from the same root cause: Spring implements @Async declaratively by wrapping the target bean in an AOP proxy (JDK dynamic proxy or CGLIB) that intercepts the call and dispatches the real execution to a task executor on a separate thread. Callers outside the bean invoke the proxy and get this async behavior correctly. But when a method inside the class calls another method annotated @Async using an implicit or explicit `this.` reference, that call bypasses the proxy entirely and goes straight to the real object - so the method runs synchronously, on the calling thread, with the @Async annotation completely ignored (no error is thrown; it just silently doesn't behave asynchronously). The fix follows the same pattern as the @Transactional case: move the @Async method into a separate Spring-managed bean and inject/call it from there (the cleanest and most common fix, and it also improves separation of concerns), or, less commonly, obtain a self-reference to the actual proxy (e.g., by injecting ApplicationContext and calling getBean(this.getClass()), or enabling AopContext.currentProxy() via exposeProxy=true on the proxy config) and route the internal call through that reference instead of `this`.

questions.question: How would you implement retry logic with backoff for a flaky external call in Spring Boot?
questions.answer: The declarative way is Spring Retry: add the spring-retry dependency, enable it with @EnableRetry, and annotate the method making the flaky call with @Retryable, specifying which exceptions should trigger a retry (retryFor = {SocketException.class, TimeoutException.class} - retrying on exceptions that indicate a business/validation failure rather than a transient infrastructure problem is a common mistake to avoid) and a maxAttempts count. The @Backoff sub-annotation controls the delay between attempts: a fixed delay (delay = 1000, wait 1 second between every attempt), or exponential backoff (delay = 1000, multiplier = 2, optionally capped with maxDelay) which doubles the wait time after each failed attempt - this matters because a fixed short delay under a real outage just hammers the struggling downstream service repeatedly, while exponential backoff progressively backs off and gives the dependency room to recover, and adding random = true jitters the delay slightly to avoid many client instances retrying in lockstep ('thundering herd'). You pair @Retryable with a @Recover method (matching the same return type, plus the triggering exception as its first parameter) that runs once all retry attempts are exhausted, letting you return a fallback value or raise a final error cleanly instead of letting the last exception propagate raw. An alternative, often used in microservices already on Resilience4j for circuit breakers, is Resilience4j's own @Retry annotation/RetryConfig, which offers the same exponential-backoff behavior and composes naturally with a CircuitBreaker (in the standard composition order, retries happen inside the circuit breaker, so exhausted retries count as a single failure toward the breaker's failure threshold).

questions.question: What is Spring Cloud OpenFeign, and how does it simplify calling other services compared to WebClient or RestTemplate?
questions.answer: OpenFeign (originally from Netflix, now maintained under Spring Cloud) is a declarative HTTP client: instead of writing imperative code that builds a request, calls it, and deserializes the response (as you do with RestTemplate or WebClient), you define a plain Java interface annotated with the target service's mapping information, and Spring generates a working implementation for you at runtime. For example, @FeignClient(name = "inventory-service") interface InventoryClient { @GetMapping("/api/inventory/{sku}") InventoryDto getBySku(@PathVariable String sku); } - you then simply @Autowired the interface and call inventoryClient.getBySku(sku) as if it were a local method; Feign handles building the HTTP request, serialization/deserialization, and (when paired with Spring Cloud LoadBalancer or Eureka) service-discovery-based load balancing across instances of the target service, all without you writing any of that plumbing. Compared to RestTemplate, the main win is drastically less boilerplate and a self-documenting client contract expressed as an interface. Compared to WebClient, Feign is (by default) synchronous/blocking rather than reactive, so it's the natural choice for traditional Spring MVC microservices that aren't otherwise using a reactive stack - using WebClient in that context just to call one downstream service adds reactive-programming complexity without a corresponding benefit. Feign also integrates cleanly with Resilience4j (via feign-circuitbreaker or fallback classes) for per-client circuit breaking and fallback behavior, and supports request/response interceptors for cross-cutting concerns like propagating an Authorization header or a correlation ID to downstream calls.

questions.question: How do you mock an external HTTP dependency in a Spring Boot integration test (e.g., with WireMock)?
questions.answer: For a pure unit test of a service that calls another component (e.g., a WebClient-wrapping client bean), the simplest approach is @MockBean to replace that client bean in the Spring context with a Mockito mock and stub its return value directly - fast, but it doesn't exercise any real HTTP serialization/deserialization or verify the actual request shape your code sends. For a more realistic integration test that verifies the real HTTP call - headers, query params, request body, response parsing - WireMock is the standard tool: it spins up an actual local HTTP server (in-process, on a random or fixed port) that you configure with stubbed responses for specific request patterns (WireMock.stubFor(WireMock.get("/inventory/123").willReturn(WireMock.aResponse().withStatus(200).withBody("..."))))), and you point your application's base URL configuration at that local WireMock server for the duration of the test (often via @DynamicPropertySource or a test-specific application-test.yml). This lets you write a genuine integration test - your real HTTP client code runs, hits a real (but fake) server, over real sockets - without depending on a flaky or rate-limited third-party service being available during CI, and lets you assert your code sends the correct request shape (verify(getRequestedFor(urlEqualTo("/inventory/123")))), not just that it correctly handles a given response. WireMock's Spring Boot integration (or the JUnit 5 WireMockExtension) can also start/stop the mock server automatically as part of the test lifecycle rather than managing it manually.

questions.question: How do liveness and readiness probes work with Spring Boot Actuator on Kubernetes, and why should they check different things?
questions.answer: Spring Boot Actuator exposes dedicated health groups for Kubernetes at /actuator/health/liveness and /actuator/health/readiness (automatically enabled when Boot detects it's running inside a Kubernetes environment, or explicitly via management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true), backed by the LivenessState and ReadinessState of the application, which Spring updates automatically as part of its own lifecycle (an app is 'live' as soon as the ApplicationContext has successfully refreshed, and 'ready' once that plus any CommandLineRunner/ApplicationRunner beans have completed). Kubernetes uses these two checks for fundamentally different purposes and, critically, they should check different things: the liveness probe answers 'is this process healthy enough that it should keep running, or is it in a broken state that only a restart can fix' - Kubernetes kills and restarts the pod if this fails, so it should only reflect unrecoverable internal problems (a deadlock, an unrecoverable state), not transient external dependency issues. The readiness probe answers 'is this instance currently able to serve traffic' - Kubernetes removes the pod from the Service's load-balancing rotation (without killing it) if this fails, so it should reflect things that make an otherwise-healthy instance temporarily unfit to receive traffic, such as a downstream database or dependency being briefly unreachable, or the app still warming up caches at startup. The critical mistake to avoid is wiring your database's health check into the liveness probe: if the database goes down, that would make Kubernetes conclude every instance is 'unhealthy' and restart them all in a loop, which does nothing to fix a database outage and just adds churn - a database check belongs in readiness (temporarily pull the pod from traffic) rather than liveness (kill and restart the pod).

questions.question: What is Spring Cloud Config, and what problem does it solve for microservices?
questions.answer: Spring Cloud Config provides server-side and client-side support for centralized, externalized configuration across a distributed system. Instead of each microservice bundling its own configuration files and requiring a rebuild/redeploy to change a setting, a Config Server exposes configuration (typically backed by a version-controlled Git repository, though it also supports a plain file system, Vault, and other backends) over HTTP, and each microservice acts as a Config Client that fetches its configuration from that server at startup, using the same property-file/YAML mechanisms it already understands. This solves several real problems in a microservices architecture: consistent, version-controlled configuration across many services and environments (dev/staging/prod) in one auditable place rather than scattered across each service's repo; the ability to update configuration for many running instances without rebuilding or redeploying application artifacts; and (combined with @RefreshScope on beans that need to pick up new values, plus a call to the Actuator /actuator/refresh endpoint, or Spring Cloud Bus for broadcasting that refresh signal to every instance in one action instead of hitting each instance's endpoint individually) the ability to change configuration at runtime - e.g., toggling a feature flag or adjusting a rate limit - without any downtime. The trade-off is architectural complexity: the Config Server itself becomes a critical piece of shared infrastructure that every other service depends on at startup, so it needs its own availability/resilience story (clients typically fail fast or fall back to a locally cached copy of the last successfully fetched configuration if the Config Server is temporarily unreachable).

questions.question: Explain how Spring AOP creates proxies (JDK dynamic proxies vs. CGLIB), and what limitations this has for advice on final classes or self-invocation.
questions.answer: Spring AOP is proxy-based (unlike AspectJ's compile-time/load-time weaving), and at container startup it decides between two proxy strategies for any bean that needs advice applied (from @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @PreAuthorize, custom @Aspect classes, etc.). If the target bean implements at least one interface, Spring by default uses a JDK dynamic proxy - built into the JDK's java.lang.reflect.Proxy, which generates a proxy class implementing the same interface(s) at runtime and routes every call through an InvocationHandler; the practical limitation is that only methods declared on the implemented interface(s) are proxied, so any method not on the interface - including any concrete, non-interface method - simply isn't advised. If the target bean does not implement any interface (or Spring Boot's default behavior, since Spring Boot sets spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true by default, always uses CGLIB for both @Transactional and @Cacheable regardless of interfaces), Spring uses a CGLIB proxy: a runtime-generated subclass of the target class, created via bytecode manipulation, that overrides methods to inject the advice logic before delegating to super. Because CGLIB works via subclassing, it has real, hard limitations: a class marked final cannot be proxied at all (you can't subclass a final class), and any individual method marked final cannot be advised even on a non-final class (you can't override a final method) - in both cases, Spring either silently skips applying the aspect or fails at startup depending on the scenario, and this is a genuine, easy-to-miss production bug (marking a @Service class or method final and being surprised that @Transactional silently does nothing). Private methods have the same problem for a different reason: proxies (both JDK and CGLIB) only intercept calls that go through the proxy's public method dispatch, so a private method can never be advised regardless of proxy type. The other well-known limitation, self-invocation, follows from the same mechanism: any call made from within the bean using `this.someMethod()` goes directly to the real object, completely bypassing the proxy and any advice attached to it - this is why @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, and method-security annotations all silently 'don't work' when called internally rather than from an external caller. Notably, AspectJ (used as an alternative in a small minority of Spring apps) doesn't have this self-invocation problem at all, because it weaves advice directly into the target class's bytecode at compile-time or load-time rather than wrapping it in a runtime proxy - but virtually no Spring Boot application uses that mode by default, so proxy-based limitations are the practical reality most teams live with.

questions.question: When would you choose Spring WebFlux over Spring MVC, and what are the practical costs of going reactive?
questions.answer: Spring MVC uses a one-thread-per-request, blocking I/O model (built on the Servlet API, running on Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow by default), which is simple to write, debug, and reason about - code reads top-to-bottom, and a blocking JDBC call or RestTemplate call is fine because the thread's entire job is to sit and wait. Spring WebFlux, introduced in Spring 5, is a fully non-blocking, reactive-stack alternative built on Project Reactor (Mono/Flux) and typically running on Netty, using a small, fixed event-loop thread pool that can handle many more concurrent in-flight requests than MVC's bounded thread pool, because a thread is never blocked waiting on I/O - while waiting for a slow downstream call, it's freed to process other requests. You'd choose WebFlux when your workload is genuinely I/O-bound with massive concurrency (an API gateway fanning out to dozens of downstream services in parallel, a system serving huge numbers of long-lived connections like Server-Sent Events or streaming), and - critically - when you can use non-blocking drivers end-to-end (WebClient instead of RestTemplate, R2DBC instead of JDBC/JPA, reactive Redis/Mongo clients); mixing WebFlux's non-blocking model with a blocking JDBC/Hibernate call anywhere in the chain defeats the purpose and can actually make things worse, since that blocking call now ties up one of WebFlux's few event-loop threads instead of one of MVC's many. The practical costs of going reactive are real and significant: the entire codebase must be written in the reactive style (Mono/Flux chains rather than plain objects and imperative control flow), which has a steep learning curve, makes debugging harder (stack traces through reactive operator chains are much less readable than a normal call stack), and often requires rewriting or replacing libraries that only offer blocking APIs (many ORMs, some legacy clients). Java 21's virtual threads have narrowed the practical gap for the 'I want to scale under blocking I/O' use case specifically - Spring MVC with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true now gets much of WebFlux's scalability benefit while keeping the simpler, blocking-style programming model - so the strongest remaining case for WebFlux specifically is genuinely reactive, backpressure-aware streaming scenarios, not just 'we want to handle more concurrent requests.'

questions.question: How would you design a rate limiter and a bulkhead for a Spring Boot service using Resilience4j, and what failure mode does each protect against?
questions.answer: A RateLimiter and a Bulkhead solve different problems, even though both cap 'how much a resource can be used.' RateLimiter (@RateLimiter(name="myApi")) restricts the number of calls permitted per time window (e.g., limitForPeriod = 10, limitRefreshPeriod = 1s means at most 10 calls/second) - its purpose is to protect against exceeding a fixed capacity contract, either your own service's ability to sustain load, or a downstream/third-party API's rate limit that would otherwise return 429s or ban your client entirely if you exceed it. When the limit is exceeded, calls either wait up to a configurable timeout for a permit to free up or are rejected immediately with a RequestNotPermitted exception, typically handled via a fallback method. Bulkhead (@Bulkhead(name="myService")) restricts the number of concurrent (simultaneous, in-flight) calls to a component, regardless of how fast or slow they are - its purpose is failure isolation: preventing one slow or overwhelmed dependency from consuming all available threads/resources and starving unrelated parts of the application (the classic 'one struggling downstream service takes down the whole app' cascading failure). Resilience4j offers two Bulkhead implementations: a SemaphoreBulkhead, which runs the call on the calling thread and uses a java.util.concurrent.Semaphore to cap concurrent access - simple, low overhead, works across any threading/I/O model, but doesn't isolate the actual execution onto separate threads; and a ThreadPoolBulkhead, which routes calls onto a dedicated, bounded thread pool with its own bounded queue - this gives true resource isolation (that dependency's calls can never consume threads meant for anything else) at the cost of an extra thread-hop and more configuration (core/max pool size, queue capacity). In a real design: you'd typically put a RateLimiter in front of calls to a rate-limited third-party API (protect against exceeding their contract) and a ThreadPoolBulkhead around calls to a downstream service whose latency is unpredictable or historically prone to spiking (protect your own thread pool from being exhausted by that one dependency) - and both compose naturally with a CircuitBreaker and Retry in the same call chain, since together they address complementary failure modes: rate limiting protects a shared resource from being overwhelmed by your own traffic, bulkheading isolates the blast radius of one dependency's slowness, and circuit breaking stops calling a dependency that's already failing.

questions.question: How would you implement idempotent message consumption in a Spring Boot Kafka consumer, given at-least-once delivery semantics?
questions.answer: Kafka's default and most commonly used delivery mode is at-least-once: with auto-commit disabled and offsets committed only after successful processing, a message will never be silently lost, but it will occasionally be redelivered - a consumer crash after processing but before committing its offset, a rebalance moving a partition mid-processing, or a producer retry after an ack was lost, all produce duplicates in practice, not just in theory. Rather than chasing Kafka's exactly-once semantics (which requires transactional producers, read_committed consumers, and coordinated two-phase-commit-style infrastructure, and only guarantees exactly-once for the Kafka-to-Kafka portion of a pipeline, not for side effects like calling an external API or writing to an external database), the pragmatic and far more common approach is to make the consumer idempotent, so that processing the same message multiple times produces the same end result as processing it once. The standard pattern: extract a stable idempotency key from each message - either a business-level identifier explicitly included in the message payload (an orderId, a paymentId), or, if no natural key exists, the message's own topic-partition-offset as a fallback (simple, but breaks if the same logical event is ever replayed from a different offset, e.g., after a topic recreation) - and before executing the side-effecting logic, check whether that key has already been processed. The most robust implementation uses the database itself as the deduplication store: an insert into a processed_messages table with the idempotency key as a UNIQUE/PRIMARY KEY constraint, executed in the same local transaction as the actual business-logic write, so that a duplicate delivery's insert simply violates the constraint and is caught/ignored - no distributed coordination needed, and it composes naturally with the transactional-outbox pattern if the consumer's processing also needs to emit further events. For higher-throughput scenarios where a database round-trip per message is too slow, a fast external store like Redis (checking/setting a key with a TTL) is a common alternative, trading perfect consistency guarantees for latency. The key interview point: 'exactly-once' is achievable but expensive and narrowly scoped; 'idempotent consumer + at-least-once delivery' is the pragmatic default that most production Kafka systems actually use.

questions.question: How do you write a custom Spring Boot auto-configuration and package it as a reusable starter?
questions.answer: A custom starter is typically split into two modules by convention: an autoconfigure module (e.g., acme-spring-boot-autoconfigure) containing the actual configuration logic, and a thin starter module (acme-spring-boot-starter) that has no code of its own and just declares the dependencies needed to use the feature (the autoconfigure module plus whatever third-party library it wraps) - this separation lets other projects depend on just the autoconfigure jar directly without pulling in the starter's opinionated dependency set, if they want finer control. The autoconfigure module contains a normal @Configuration class annotated (typically with proxyBeanMethods = false for a small startup performance win, since auto-configuration classes usually don't need CGLIB-proxied @Bean methods calling each other) with conditional annotations that make it 'back off' cleanly when not applicable or already customized - @ConditionalOnClass(SomeThirdPartyClient.class) so the configuration only applies when the relevant library is actually on the classpath, @ConditionalOnMissingBean so a user-defined bean of the same type always wins over the auto-configured default, and often @ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "acme", name = "enabled", havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true) to let users toggle the feature off entirely via configuration. You typically pair the configuration class with an @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "acme") class exposing tunable settings, registered via @EnableConfigurationProperties(AcmeProperties.class). To actually be discovered by Spring Boot's auto-configuration mechanism, the configuration class must be listed in a META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports file inside the jar (in modern Spring Boot; older versions used a spring.factories entry under the org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.EnableAutoConfiguration key) - Spring Boot's annotation processor can also generate a META-INF/spring-autoconfigure-metadata.properties file that lets Boot eagerly filter out non-matching auto-configurations before even loading their classes, improving startup time. The overall design goal, matching Spring Boot's own philosophy, is that the starter should apply useful defaults automatically when its prerequisites are met, but never fight a user who has explicitly configured something themselves - every piece of auto-configured behavior should be easy to override or disable.

questions.question: Explain how Hibernate's first-level and second-level caches interact with a Spring-managed transaction, and where they can cause stale-data bugs.
questions.answer: The first-level cache (L1) is the Hibernate Session's own identity map - it's mandatory, always on, cannot be disabled, and is scoped strictly to a single Session (which in a typical Spring app corresponds to one transaction, when using JpaTransactionManager). Within that one transaction, if you load the same entity by ID twice, Hibernate returns the exact same in-memory Java object from the L1 cache on the second call rather than re-querying the database - this is what guarantees that within a transaction, entity identity is consistent (two references to 'the same row' really are the same object) and prevents redundant queries within one unit of work. Because it's tied to the Session, L1 offers zero protection or risk across transactions: it's cleared/discarded when the Session closes at the end of the transaction, so there's no possibility of L1 alone causing stale reads in a later, separate transaction. The second-level cache (L2) is optional, must be explicitly enabled (hibernate.cache.use_second_level_cache=true plus a cache provider like Ehcache, Caffeine, Infinispan, or Hazelcast, and entities individually opted in via @Cacheable/@org.hibernate.annotations.Cache), and is shared across all Sessions within the same SessionFactory (i.e., across every transaction and every request in the running application, and - if using a distributed cache provider - potentially across multiple application instances). This is where stale-data bugs actually become possible: L2 has a chosen concurrency strategy (READ_ONLY for data that truly never changes; READ_WRITE, which uses soft locks/versioning for a reasonable consistency/performance balance; NONSTRICT_READ_WRITE, which updates the cache after commit with no locking, meaning there's a real window where a concurrent reader can see stale data; or TRANSACTIONAL, which needs a JTA-aware cache provider for the strongest consistency at the highest overhead) - pick the wrong strategy for how often the entity actually changes, and readers across different transactions can see outdated data for a period of time. The most dangerous and easy-to-miss stale-data scenario, called out explicitly by Hibernate's own documentation, is that the second-level cache is entirely unaware of any change made outside Hibernate's control - a direct SQL UPDATE run against the database (a manual data-fix script, a separate application or service writing to the same tables without going through this same Hibernate SessionFactory) leaves the L2 cache holding the old value indefinitely, since nothing ever told Hibernate to invalidate that entry; the fix is either avoiding out-of-band writes entirely, or programmatically evicting the relevant cache region (Cache.evictEntityData(...)) whenever such an external write is known to happen. In a Spring context specifically, the practical guidance is: L1 is safe and requires no thought since it's transaction-scoped by design; L2 is a genuine trade-off between performance and consistency, and should only be enabled for entities where you've deliberately decided the read-performance win is worth the risk of briefly stale data, never turned on blindly for every entity.
